title: Automating Cyber Risk Assessment With Public LLMs: An Expert-Validated Framework and Comparative Analysis
authors: Unal N.M.; Celiktas B.
abstract: Traditional cyber risk assessment methodologies face a critical dilemma: they are either quantitative yet static and context-agnostic (e.g., CVSS), or context-aware yet highly labor-intensive and subjective (e.g., NIST SP 800-30). Consequently, organizations struggle to scale risk assessment to match the pace of evolving threats. This paper presents an automated, context-aware risk assessment framework that leverages the reasoning capabilities of publicly available Large Language Models (LLMs) to operationalize expert knowledge. Rather than positioning the LLM as the final decision-maker, the framework decouples semantic interpretation from risk scoring authority through a transparent, deterministic Dynamic Metric Engine. Unlike complex closed box machine learning models, our approach anchors the AI's reasoning to this expert-validated metric schema, with weights derived using the Rank Order Centroid (ROC) method from a survey of 101 cybersecurity professionals. We evaluated the framework through a comparative study involving 15 diverse real-world vulnerability scenarios (C<inf>1</inf>-C<inf>15</inf>) and three supplementary sensitivity stress tests (C<inf>16</inf>-C<inf>18</inf>). The validation scenarios were independently assessed by a cohort of ten senior human experts and two state-of-the-art LLM agents (GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Flash). The results show that the LLM-driven agents achieve scoring consistency closely aligned with the human median (Pearson r ranging from 0.9390 to 0.9717, Spearman ρ from 0.8472 to 0.9276) against a highly reliable expert baseline (Cronbach's α =0.996), while reducing the assessment cycle time by more than 100× (averaging under 4 seconds per case vs. a human average of 6 minutes). Furthermore, a dedicated context sensitivity analysis (C<inf>13</inf>-C<inf>15</inf>) indicates that the framework adapts risk scores based on organizational context (e.g., SME vs. Critical Infrastructure) for identical technical vulnerabilities. Importantly, the system is designed not merely to replicate expert intuition, but to enforce bounded, policy-consistent risk evaluation under predefined governance constraints. Overall, these findings suggest that commercially available LLMs, when constrained by expert-validated metric schemas, can support reproducible, transparent, and real-time risk assessments.

title: Out of time for the version of record: designing living knowledge infrastructure for AI-accelerated scholarship
authors: AlAhmad H.
abstract: Dominant publishing workflows took shape under conditions of relative epistemic stability: slower problem cycles, bounded corpora, and institutions better able to absorb delay. Those conditions now hold unevenly, and in many fast-moving fields they no longer match the tempo of the object itself. Claims can become decision-relevant within days or weeks, while formal validation still unfolds over months. The result is a widening gap between what begins to circulate with authority and what has actually been epistemically stabilised. This article treats generative AI not as the origin of that problem, nor as a substitute for scholarly judgement, but as an intensifier of pressures already building within contemporary systems of validation. Using conceptual-design research, it identifies recurring breakdown patterns in scholarly publishing and translates them into explicit design requirements. From there, it proposes Living Knowledge Infrastructure (LKI) as a redesign of scholarly validation for an era in which generative AI accelerates knowledge production faster than existing publishing systems can verify it. It advances a sociotechnical framework for sustaining cumulative verification beyond the version of record. The contribution is architectural and testable: LKI links pedagogical review, executable knowledge, journals as knowledge stewards, and epistemic care into a model designed to preserve review continuity, lower verification costs, and strengthen corrigibility under accelerated conditions. Rather than calling simply for faster or more open dissemination, the article argues for a linked redesign of how scholarly judgement is recorded, carried across versions, and made publicly accountable when uptake begins to outrun validation.

title: Prompting Africa, hearing the West: generative AI music, sonic data coloniality and the future of culturally accountable musical intelligence
authors: Addaquay A.P.
abstract: Generative music systems are being increasingly recognised as adaptable creative technologies that can generate entire compositions, vocal components, instrumental layers, and stylistic variations based on text prompts, uploaded audio, and customised model conditioning. This article contends that such assertions necessitate thorough examination when pertaining to African music and the varied musical traditions, hybrid practices, and performance contexts encompassed by the term. The concern is not that modern AI music systems are incapable of producing outputs that mimic African music. They frequently represent Africanness using recognisable sonic markers such as dense percussion, chant-like vocals, generic “Afro” grooves, pentatonic colour, ululation, and tropicalised production. However, they do not adequately capture the performance systems that render specific African musical practices culturally, linguistically, and socially comprehensible. Utilising African musicology, music information retrieval, decolonial AI, dataset criticism, and digital cultural heritage, this article articulates the notion of sonic data coloniality to analyse the processes through which musical cultures are collected, classified, abstracted, trained, generated, and monetised within disparate technological frameworks. It further posits cultural competence, rather than purity, as the suitable criterion for evaluating AI-generated African music. The article presents a framework for musicological evaluation that is based on prompts and reference audio. This framework encompasses generic prompts, culturally specific prompts, expert prompts, and source-conditioned workflows, utilising rights-cleared African recordings. It posits that evaluation should consider vocality, tone-language relationships, rhythm, groove, microtiming, instrumental idiom, call-and-response, dance implications, social functions, consent, and benefit-sharing. The article asserts that African music ought to be integrated into AI systems not as a homogenised continental sound but rather through the distinct traditions, hybrid practices, performance expertise, and cultural authorities that imbue it with significance.

title: Generative grounded theory (GGT): Inductive theory building in the age of generative AI
authors: Schmitt B.; Hao S.; Pham M.T.; Hofstetter R.
abstract: This paper introduces generative grounded theory (GGT), an AI-enhanced method for inductive theory building that adapts grounded theory—and qualitative research procedures more broadly—to contemporary digital and algorithmic research conditions. GGT integrates generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into grounded-theory analysis while preserving human interpretive authority and theoretical responsibility. The method specifies a step-by-step process that supports systematic comparison and structured engagement with qualitative data. We demonstrate the method by outlining two new consumer-psychology studies and reanalyzing two established grounded-theory studies. We also address concerns surrounding GenAI use and outline future developments in the use of GenAI for qualitative analyses. GGT enables greater scale and efficiency in working with qualitative data, which are increasingly heterogeneous and multimodal, while supporting rigorous and precise theory construction and enhancing transparency and traceability. GGT can also be extended to other qualitative approaches that rely on similar analytic procedures.

title: When machines explain medicine: Nursing ethics and clinical communication
authors: Yang X.; Liang Y.; Liu Y.; Liu D.; Yang L.; Zhang B.; Xu C.; Wu Y.; He J.
abstract: Clinical communication is ethically consequential, shaping how diagnostic information is interpreted, trusted, and acted upon. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to reformulate technical reports into patient-facing explanations. Although such ‘plain-language’ outputs can improve comprehension and reduce communication workload, their ethical implications for everyday clinical communication, particularly in nursing practice, remain underexamined. This article provides a normative ethical analysis of how LLM-mediated explanations reshape clinical communication. It addresses three interrelated questions: how automated explanation redistributes interpretive authority among clinicians, nurses, patients, and algorithmic systems; how this redistribution affects responsibility and accountability; and how LLM-mediated explanations influence the ethical communication of uncertainty and trust in routine care. The analysis is informed by peer-reviewed empirical studies published between 2022 and 2025 on LLM-assisted explanation in radiology and pathology communication, identified through a focused, non-systematic search of major biomedical databases. Drawing on this literature, the article examines how automated explanation reshapes clinical meaning-making in contexts characterised by informational complexity and diagnostic uncertainty. Across existing studies, a consistent pattern emerges: as explanation becomes partially automated and more widely accessible, interpretive framing increasingly occurs outside clinician–patient dialogue, including through workflow-integrated tools and patient-side consultation. Interpretive authority is thus distributed across clinicians, nurses, patients, and platform-based systems, while formal accountability remains concentrated within professional roles. We argue that LLM-assisted explanation should be understood as mediation rather than neutral translation, raising important ethical questions about interpretive authority, responsibility, and the representation of uncertainty in clinical communication.

title: Building an Autonomous Cyber Defense System Through Generative AI Framework
authors: Dcosta R.; Pervez S.; Hosseini S.E.
abstract: This research develops and evaluates the D-GEN-SOC, a Security Operation Center (SOC) framework that is defensively oriented and combines open-source telemetry (Wazuh), incident coordination (The Hive), and a lightweight AI augmentation grounded in explainable automation. The project prototypes a modular architecture that is designed for transparent, ethical, and auditable SOC decision support. This study adopted a Design Science Research (DSR) approach to design, implement and evaluate the D-GEN-SOC framework. A controlled lab environment was deployed on an Ubuntu-based system to simulate realistic activity and generate attack that were synthetic, such as SSH brute-force attempts. These performances were consumed by Wazuh, analysed, and automatically forwarded to TheHive using a Python-based connector. A local AI module that summarizes those alerts using Gemini 1.5's free-tier API, which creates a small summary report that is stored alongside for analyst and human-in-the-loop (HITL) validation. The assessment scripts measured the Mean Time to Detect (MTTD) and alert-forwarding latency across 20 alerts, and a prototype was achieved with an MTTD of 84.83s and a Wazuh → TheHive latency of 29.55 s, demonstrating a near-real-time detection and a reliable coordination between the SIEM and SOAR layers. This visualization also includes a timeline graph and a histogram that reveals a stable sub-minute response cycle. During the experiments, the Cortex analyser layer was unstable, and the results confirmed that even partial AI augmentation, log summarization, prioritization, and metrics computation can improve the explainability and readiness for analyst without replacing the human authority. D-GEN-SOC offers a culturally aligned blueprint for NZ organizations to integrate AI within open-source SOC ecosystems. The findings also demonstrated the measures that improved MTTD by ∼53%), MTTR by ( 4 0 %), and fewer false-positive reductions by (10 %), validating the framework' s operational feasibility.

title: Should Machines Get to Judge? Rethinking the Design of AI-Mediated Assessment in Education
authors: Pauzi Z.; Mavrikis M.
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) approaches, particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), are increasingly being proposed as automated assessors, motivated by measurable gains in efficiency and consistency. Yet these advantages do not resolve a central question: should systems with known limitations be granted evaluative authority over learners? Drawing on a critical review of recent studies, we identify persistent issues, including bias, opacity, reliability gaps, and accountability voids. We also review existing policies and standards to further understand how the gap between reported evidences and what is expected can be closed. Delegating judgment to LLMs is not a neutral technical improvement; it constitutes a significant redistribution of power within education. We argue that, when and if AI is used in assessment, it should be framed as a site of human-AI negotiation at all times rather than automated decision-making. We outline design recommendations to close this gap, particularly by prioritising pedagogical value and human oversight. By addressing the rapid normalisation of algorithmic authority, we call on the community to confront the ethical and pedagogical stakes of machine judgment and to design systems that preserve the agency of students and teachers.

query_string: TITLE-ABS-KEY(("generative AI" OR "large language model" OR ChatGPT) AND (authority OR deference))
title: Hybrid Intelligence
authors: Lutz C.; Newlands G.; Jarrahi M.H.
abstract: This chapter offers a comprehensive overview of hybrid intelligence, through which humans collaborate with artificial intelligence (AI) systems to enhance human and AI capabilities while ensuring that human values, needs, and authority remain central. In line with the principles of Human-Centered AI (HCAI), hybrid intelligence leverages the complementary strengths of humans and AI to create systems that augment, rather than replace, human decision-making and creativity. The chapter discusses how hybrid intelligence prioritizes human oversight, controllability, authority, and ethical considerations, ensuring that AI serves to enhance human well-being and aligns with societal values. It also addresses recent technological advancements, including foundation models, which have highlighted the importance of hybrid intelligence in fields such as healthcare, decision support, and innovation. Alongside these developments, the chapter emphasizes critical ethical and social challenges, such as fairness, accountability, trust, and privacy, within an HCAI framework. The chapter concludes by highlighting future research directions that integrate technical, social, and ethical perspectives to create sustainable, human-centered hybrid intelligence systems that prioritize human agency oversight as well as ethical design.

title: GOVERNING AI-ASSISTED ASSESSMENT IN MARKETING EDUCATION: A ROLE-BASED TYPOLOGY AND PRATICAL GUIDELINES
authors: Bello R.
abstract: This article examines how marketing educators and programs can govern artificial intelligence (AI) used for assessing student work. AI denotes the broader category of computational systems that predict, classify, interpret, or support decisions; generative AI (GenAI) denotes the subset of those systems that produces new content, such as feedback, rubric interpretations, assessment summaries, and grade rationales. The distinction matters because governance requirements follow from the authority an output is permitted to exercise rather than from whether the system is generative. Marketing provides a particularly revealing context because its assessments often require students to integrate analytical evidence, creative choice, audience-sensitive communication, and defensible managerial judgment. Drawing on research on marketing education, assessment, legitimacy, procedural justice, and algorithmic judgment, the article develops a role-based typology of AI-assisted assessment. The typology distinguishes five roles (Assistant, Evaluator, Arbiter, Monitor, and Governor) according to the authority AI exercises over assessment judgment and the scope across which its consequences extend. Legitimacy determines the governance burden associated with each role, including requirements for explanation, oversight, evidence, accountability, and contestability. The article then provides practical guidelines for classifying AI uses and determining whether a particular role is defensible given the learning objective, assessment stakes, and institutional context.

title: Evaluating the Safety of Local LLM-Generated Exercise Prescriptions Against Clinical Guidelines
authors: De Mendonca A.M.P.; Pessoa Sousa F.; Coelho I.M.
abstract: Large language models are increasingly employed as fitness coaching tools, yet their ability to generate clinically safe exercise plans, particularly for individuals with chronic conditions, remains largely unexplored. Based on a complementary literature search, this work presents the first fully deterministic audit of exercise plans generated by four local open-source LLMs running entirely on consumer-grade hardware via Ollama, without commercial API dependencies. A total of 288 plans spanning eight patient profiles and three prompt authority framings were evaluated against 15 criteria grounded in ACSM, WHO, ADA, and AHA clinical guidelines. The experiments reveal a safety-calibration paradox: all models achieve high safety scores yet systematically fail at age-stratified intensity calibration, a limitation that persists regardless of model size or clinical specialization. Furthermore, prompt authority framing significantly modulates both safety alignment and refusal behavior. These findings suggest that local LLMs can produce structurally complete exercise plans at lower cost than commercial alternatives, but require complementary rule-based intensity verification before deployment in clinical or digital health settings. All source code and datasets are publicly available.

title: AI in education influencers: Problematising, reproducing, or mediating the technological solutionism discourse in UK schools?
authors: Bekirsky L.
abstract: This study explores the pivotal role of AI in education micro-influencers in shaping the discourse around generative AI tools in UK education. Drawing from social network analysis, discourse analysis, and interviews with key influencers, the research reveals how influencers navigate the trade-off between credibility and monetisation while serving as brokers between educators, edtech companies, and policymakers. Findings reveal that influencers are central to online and offline networks around this topic, using a range of strategies to promote their services and foster discussion. While influencers often endorse and promote AI as a tool to reduce teacher workload, many are cautious of over-promising, striving to maintain credibility through transparency and promoting ethical use. Mediating between edtech tools and practitioners, influencers may represent a shift in authority over pedagogical practice in UK schools. This study highlights the influencers’ dual role as advocates and critical voices within an increasingly commercialised educational landscape.

title: AI and the Rule and Role of Law: Reshaping Legal Regulatory Frameworks to Address Emerging Challenges
authors: Chung C.H.
abstract: The rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies—especially Generative AI and autonomous systems—has fundamentally challenged the foundations of legal governance, raising critical questions about the rule of law and the capacity of regulatory frameworks to ensure legal certainty, accountability, and enforceability. While existing legal scholarship has primarily focused on sector-specific AI regulations and compliance mechanisms, it has largely overlooked the broader implications of AI on legal authority, governance structures, and institutional legitimacy. This study addresses this gap by critically examining how AI disrupts traditional legal paradigms, weakens enforcement mechanisms, and reshapes regulatory authority. It argues that AI’s autonomy, algorithmic opacity, transnational reach, and unprecedented scale and speed erode state control over rule-making, overwhelm regulatory institutions, and shift governance power to private AI actors—thereby diminishing democratic accountability. Given these transformations, the study advocates for a reconfiguration of legal regulatory frameworks toward adaptive, participatory, and ethically grounded governance models capable of responding to AI’s evolving nature. By bridging legal theory and political science perspectives, this study contributes to the growing discourse on AI governance, offering a theoretical and policy-oriented framework for reasserting the role of law in regulating AI-driven, high-impact decision-making.

title: The invisible hand of generative AI: quasi-agency and knowledge transformation in data-driven decision-making
authors: Cristofaro M.; Banon-Gomis A.; Giardino P.L.
abstract: Purpose – This study aims to examine how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) reshapes knowledge management (KM) in data-driven decision-making (DDDM), reconfigures principal–agent relations and creates new challenges for epistemic governance. It focuses on how GenAI influences the construction, synthesis, justification and retention of decision-relevant knowledge across the decision cycle. Design/methodology/approach – This study adopts an abductive qualitative design, drawing on data from 120 managers at Italian small and medium-sized enterprises actively using GenAI in recurring DDDM activities. Drawing on ten open-ended questions aligned with the decision cycle, the analysis applies reflexive thematic analysis, supported by Gioia-informed coding procedures, to identify recurring phase-level governance patterns and to develop a phase-sensitive framework. Findings – This study develops a phase-sensitive model of GenAI quasi-agency showing how generative artificial intelligence reshapes organizational knowledge throughout the decision cycle. The model explains that GenAI transforms knowledge through three recurring mechanisms – knowledge coupling, knowledge decoupling and knowledge hiding – which operate with different intensity across decision phases and redefine the governance requirements for traceability, reconstructability, contestability and human justificatory ownership. Consequently, agency risks increasingly originate from the transformation of hidden knowledge rather than from hidden human action. Originality/value – This study introduces the concept of GenAI quasi-agency, defined as the capacity of GenAI systems to shape framing, evidence construction, prioritization, justification and organizational memory without possessing formal authority, intentionality or accountability. It contributes to KM by conceptualizing GenAI-supported decision-making as a problem of epistemic governance centered on preserving traceability, reconstructability, contestability and human justificatory ownership. The study also extends principal–agent theory by showing how agency risks increasingly arise from the transformation of hidden knowledge rather than from hidden action alone and develops a phase-sensitive framework that explains how governance requirements vary across the DDDM cycle.

title: The Algorithmic Native Speaker: Linguistic Racism, Generative AI and English Language Education From the Global South
authors: Veliz L.
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly becoming a language-learning partner, writing adviser, assessor, curriculum designer and source of pedagogical knowledge. Yet its expansion into English language education has largely been discussed through the languages of efficiency, innovation, personalisation and academic integrity. This conceptual article argues that such framings are inadequate for the Global South, where English education is already organised by colonial histories, racialised hierarchies of speakerhood, marketised promises of mobility and standardised proficiency regimes. Bringing raciolinguistic theory, coloniality, native-speakerism and critical work on language datafication into conversation, the article conceptualises GenAI as an algorithmic native speaker; that is, not a literal speaker, but a sociotechnical authority that models, judges and circulates idealised English while obscuring the racial, geopolitical and commercial conditions of that authority. Four interlocking operations are identified: (i) extractive datafication, (ii) probabilistic standardisation, (iii) automated evaluation and (iv) aspirational subject formation. Chile is used as a situated example of how these operations may enter a stratified English education system in which English is promoted as a route to global participation while Indigenous languages and local English practices remain comparatively marginal. The article argues that GenAI can intensify a ‘bilingual illusion’ in which linguistic modernity is imagined chiefly as movement between standard Spanish and standard English. However, these effects are not inevitable. Educators, policymakers and learners retain agency in deciding how GenAI is adopted, questioned and governed, so these operations are better understood as tendencies that can be amplified or interrupted than as fixed outcomes. The article proposes a raciolinguistically informed critical AI literacy for English language education organised around five pedagogical commitments: historicising, auditing, counter-prompting, re-voicing and collective governance. The central implication is that equitable GenAI integration requires more than detecting biased outputs. It requires transforming who is authorised to define legitimate language, knowledge and educational futures.

title: A governed framework combining large language models and human oversight for supplier selection
authors: Rezaei M.; Iyer S.S.; Fatahi Valilai O.
abstract: Supplier selection requires organisations to combine structured procurement records with evolving information on sustainability, compliance, operational risk, and market conditions. The ability to reassess suppliers as this information changes is important for maintaining responsive and resilient supply chains. This paper proposes a governed human-in-the-loop framework that connects procurement intent, supplier data, qualitative evidence, multi-criteria analysis, explanation, and managerial review. Language model components support the interpretation of sourcing requests, the extraction of source-linked evidence, and the formulation of revised decision scenarios. Deterministic services remain responsible for weighting, constraint application, scoring, and ranking, while procurement professionals approve consequential analytical and evidential choices. Partial automation of evidence processing and scenario preparation allows supplier evaluations to be updated in response to changing conditions while procurement professionals retain final decision authority. The framework is examined using public procurement records and controlled benchmarks covering scenario formulation, evidence processing, multi-criteria trade-offs, robustness, and explanation fidelity. Its design incorporates schema validation, source-level provenance, explicit evidence policies, deterministic fallbacks, and four human approval checkpoints. Using the extended procurement-fit representation increases Ref@10 from 5.259% to 31.642%; the language model components achieve a valid structured-output rate of 1.000, mean evidence-claim F1 of 0.928, and exact preservation of the fixed deterministic ranking in all explanation cases. The study contributes an auditable approach to combining the interpretive capabilities of language models with established supplier selection methods, providing a basis for more adaptive supplier evaluation while recognising the need for validation in enterprise procurement settings.

title: Beyond or within the binary? Constructing gendered meanings in generative AI use
authors: Lai Z.; Tang Y.
abstract: Introduction. GenAI is increasingly embedded in daily life, yet its ostensibly neutral design often becomes a site for gendered interpretations. This study examines how Gen Z users in China perceive and construct gendered traits in GenAI, situating their accounts within broader concerns of neutrality and equity in information society. Method. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 12 participants who regularly use multiple GenAI platforms. Discussions explored textual, visual, and auditory cues, user projections, and contextual triggers. Analysis. Thematic analysis, informed by Butler’s theory of performativity and Haraway’s cyborg imaginary, was applied to 73,480 words of transcripts. Coding identified patterns in participants’ accounts of gendered cues, user projection, contextual attribution, and reflections on neutrality. Results. Participants consistently mapped rational, didactic tones onto masculine authority and empathetic language onto feminine care. Avatars and voices anchored gender perceptions, while mimicry highlighted both adaptability and artificiality. Attribution also d rew on cultural repertoires, personal experiences, and task contexts. Conclusion. Neutrality in GenAI does not erase gender but becomes a site of projection and negotiation. The findings show how such systems can reproduce stereotypes while also enabling more inclusive, post-binary imaginaries, underscoring the need for critical AI lite racy and designs that advance information equity.

title: Disinformation governance and political expression: Comparative accountability gaps and an extended framework for independent oversight
authors: Yu J.
abstract: This article examines three major institutional approaches to disinformation governance (self-regulation, co-regulation and state-centred regulation) and assesses their implications for the protection of political expression. Through a qualitative comparative analysis of the Digital Services Act (DSA) framework in the European Union, Meta’s Oversight Board and the Korea Internet Self-governance Organization (KISO) and South Korea’s state-led regulation, the study identifies recurring accountability gaps across models, using four analytical criteria: authority allocation, independence, transparency and contestability. These weaknesses have become more acute in an environment shaped by generative AI, the politicization of large platforms and the increasing use of disinformation by state actors. Building on prior scholarship and extending existing conceptual work on institutional independence, the article develops a refined framework for independent oversight suited to the contemporary information ecosystem. This framework aims to improve checks and balances, strengthen transparency and offer more credible opportunities for review than current arrangements allow. The findings highlight the need for renewed institutional design to safeguard democratic political expression amidst accelerating technological and political risks.

title: Clinical warrant in medical LLM evaluation
authors: Sariyar M.
abstract: Medical large language models are evaluated through factuality, physician preference, source support, retrieval quality, safety, and clinical utility. These measures describe content and performance while leaving unresolved whether a generated claim meets the requirements for a specified clinical use. This article proposes clinical warrant as a use-specific judgment for a particular output–use pair. Clinical use includes reliance within a patient-related encounter, task, or care pathway, including education that can shape understanding or later action. The proposed use and the standards used to judge it are documented separately. For action-guiding outputs, clinical appropriateness is a gateway. Five further conditions examine role, case information, evidence, preserved limits, and authority/accountability. The framework asks whether these requirements are met at the point of proposed reliance, records failed or unresolved conditions and the resulting disposition, and tests whether a relevant change stops or redirects use. Fifteen constructed examples across five domains distinguish established, not established, and indeterminate warrant.

title: Delegation Across Democracies: Using AI to Study Political Institutions at Scale
authors: Jason Anastasopoulos L.; Lian J.
abstract: We introduce a framework for measuring delegation in democratic political institutions using fine-tuned large language models (LLMs). Delegation, the transfer of policymaking authority from principals to agents, is a central but challenging concept to measure across legal systems. Building on past work in rule-based natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning, we develop a unified approach that combines the interpretability of linguistic pattern matching with the adaptability of LLMs. We fine-tune legal-domain LLMs to detect delegation provisions in statutory texts and validate our approach on landmark American legislation. Our results demonstrate that even with limited computational resources, fine-tuned LLMs like LegalBERT can robustly identify delegatory provisions with high accuracy and meaningful alignment to legal language. This work enhances the ability of researchers to systematically study delegation in diverse legal and institutional settings.

title: A Risk-Governed Deployment Framework for LLM-Powered Educational Companion Robots in K - 12 Education
authors: Wu L.; Zhang M.; Zhai P.; Cao Y.
abstract: Large language models offer new possibilities for personalized learning support, but direct deployment in K-12 education remains constrained by content reliability, developmental suitability, privacy protection, and institutional accountability. These concerns become more salient when LLMs are embedded in educational companion robots, because embodiment can increase engagement and perceived authority. This paper proposes a risk-governed deployment framework for LLM-powered educational companion robots in K-12 settings. The framework combines grounded response generation, age-appropriate prompting, runtime risk grading, human-in-the-loop escalation, and feedback-based policy refinement. It defines three risk levels and links them to response constraints and supervisory actions, while organizing deployment into four stages: preparation, pilot use, institutional operation, and iterative optimization. A scenario-based pilot with 120 representative interactions suggests that the framework can balance educational usefulness, runtime safety control, and governance feasibility in child-facing deployment.

title: Authorization assurance for tool-using LLM agents: a structured review of enforcement semantics and effect-level security evidence
authors: Elmasry M.A.
abstract: Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents exercise authority over protected resources through APIs, tools, credentials, and external services. This structured review asks whether authorization claims are supported at the enforcement and observation boundaries relevant to the claimed effect. A 75-source evidence library was screened into a 30-source analytical corpus (15 strict agent sources, 6 sensitivity sources, and 9 authorization/assurance comparators), yielding 92 Source-Claim Records. Within this closed corpus, five strict sources made mediation or non-bypassability claims with heterogeneous evidence endpoints; all three evaluable least-privilege sources narrowed available authority without measuring trajectory-wide effective privilege; no evaluable revocation claim appeared among 21 agent-focused sources; and no delegation-containment claim appeared in the 30-source corpus. Final-state correctness was also distinct from authorization correctness. We integrate these findings through an Authorization Assurance Claim Model linking claim scope, obligations, enforcement, evidence, protected effect, and residual assumptions. The resulting MAAP is presented as a preliminary, review-derived minimum reporting framework, not a validated scoring or certification instrument. The supplementary workbook provides the screening decisions, complete coding dataset, source-property matrix, sensitivity analyses, and independent coding audit.

title: Governing deepfake realities: The truth immunity framework for telecommunications policy
authors: Zhang B.
abstract: The proliferation of deepfakes presents a critical telecommunications policy challenge, threatening the integrity of digital information infrastructures and eroding trust in public communication systems. While recent regulatory initiatives—such as the EU Digital Services Act (DSA) and China's Generative AI Measures—seek to strengthen platform accountability, they remain insufficiently integrated into the operational mandates and regulatory toolkits of telecommunications authorities. To address this gap, this paper proposes the Truth Immunity (TI) framework (TI = R<inf>a</inf> × Cᵤ × Ag), a policy-oriented model that conceptualizes deepfake governance failure as a systemic coordination trap among cognitive vulnerabilities, algorithmic amplification, and fragmented regulatory authority. Drawing on a comparative analysis of major deepfake incidents in China, India, and Ukraine, the study demonstrates how variations in institutional capacity shape regulatory effectiveness across crisis communication, electoral integrity, and geopolitical contexts. The TI framework advances a tripartite, multiplicative governance approach by specifying actionable pathways for enhancing Algorithmic Responsibility (R<inf>a</inf>) through phased algorithmic audits, strengthening Public Capability (Cᵤ) via digital literacy embedded in universal service frameworks, and reinforcing Governance Accountability (Ag) through structured cross-border coordination mechanisms. By translating these principles into differentiated implementation pathways for the EU, the United States, China, and India, the framework enables telecommunications regulators to embed TI instruments within existing regulatory workflows. In doing so, the study provides a structured yet adaptable policy toolkit for mitigating deepfake-driven risks and strengthening systemic resilience across diverse telecommunications governance regimes.

query_string: TITLE-ABS-KEY(("generative AI" OR "large language model" OR ChatGPT) AND (authority OR deference))
title: Acceptable English, Vanishing Voice: AI Polishing and the South- North Politics of Academic Style
authors: Rahmatullah M.
abstract: This commentary examines the growing normalisation of AI-polished academic English in South-North scholarly publishing. While generative AI may help multilingual scholars manage linguistic barriers, its uncritical use risks producing a standardised academic style that erases situated voice, local idiom, intellectual hesitation and interpretive risk. The problem, therefore, is not simply whether AI has been used, but how its use reshapes authorship, legitimacy and scholarly presence. Building on the recent Critical Arts manifesto “Being Sceptical,” the commentary argues that the journal's concern with artificial intelligence and intellectual integrity should be extended from book reviewing to the wider politics of academic style. In journals committed to cultural studies, media studies and postcolonial critique, academic style is never neutral: it carries histories of access, authority, citation and exclusion. The commentary argues that AI detection alone cannot protect intellectual integrity. Instead, journals need a situated ethics of scholarly voice: one that distinguishes language assistance from intellectual substitution, requires transparent disclosure, protects multilingual expression, and evaluates manuscripts through evidence, argument, citation accuracy and interpretive labour. The future of academic English should not be machine-made sameness, but a more capacious language able to carry difference, locality and critical thought.

title: LedgerRAG: Governance-Driven Agentic Chain of Retrieval for Dynamic Knowledge Scenarios
authors: Wang S.; Zhang Y.; Guo Y.; Kang J.
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds large language models (LLMs) with external evidence. Dynamic knowledge tasks, however, require systems to decide not only what to retrieve but also when to refresh, how to arbitrate conflicts, and how to preserve an auditable record of the evidence used to answer a query. We present LedgerRAG, a trigger-aware retrieval chain framework that maintains an explicit claim-level evidence ledger and uses coverage, temporal validity, authority, and conflict signals to control retrieval, refresh, and stopping decisions. We expand the evaluation with a query-level BM25 baseline, a dense retriever setting, and task-aligned proxy baselines representing graph-style retrieval, temporal-only retrieval, and conflict-focused retrieval. The revised results show that LedgerRAG’s clearest advantage lies in conflict governance and auditable evidence control, achieving near-perfect ConFLICT adjudication (CRAcc = 0.993) under authority-aware routing while yielding more modest gains and explicit trade-offs in regulation-change and streaming settings.

title: Toward autonomous decision support in semiconductor manufacturing: a review of planning, scheduling, dispatching, and execution control
authors: Li L.; Li Y.; Tang J.; Yu Q.
abstract: Semiconductor manufacturing is a high-stakes cyber-physical production domain in which planning targets, scheduling feasibility, dispatching actions, process-control feedback, and human oversight must remain continuously aligned. This paper presents a structured state-of-the-art review of semiconductor smart manufacturing from the perspective of autonomous intelligent systems (AIS). The review does not treat planning, scheduling, dispatching, real-time dispatching (RTD), advanced process control (APC), manufacturing execution systems (MES), advanced planning and scheduling (APS), and enterprise resource planning (ERP) as separate production-management topics. Instead, it synthesizes them as bounded components of a human-supervised closed-loop decision architecture. The central artifact is an AIS reference model that maps fab layers to state inputs, decision-support functions, human authority, and audit or safeguard mechanisms. The review also develops a deployment-maturity matrix for classical optimization, simulation, rule-based dispatching, predictive learning, reinforcement learning, digital twins, LLM-enabled orchestration, and industrial software infrastructure. The synthesis shows that classical methods remain central because they provide interpretable constraints and executable interfaces. Learning-based and large-language-model-enabled methods can strengthen state estimation, policy adaptation, semantic mediation, and human-system interaction, but only under validated simulation or offline evaluation, bounded authority, safe fallback, access control, and auditable records. Semiconductor fabs should therefore not be described as fully autonomous systems. A more defensible AIS framing is trustworthy, human-supervised autonomous decision support: systems that sense changing fab states, evaluate alternatives, recommend or execute approved actions, and feed outcomes back into planning, scheduling, dispatching, and process-control decisions.

query_string: TITLE-ABS-KEY(("generative AI" OR "large language model" OR ChatGPT) AND (authority OR deference))
title: Artificial Intelligence in Human Resource Management:Transforming Workforce Optimization, Recruitment, and Employee Engagement
authors: Arora S.; Srivastava R.; Gupta V.K.
abstract: - Artificial intelligence (AI), which enhances workforce optimization, decision-making, and process automation, is transforming human resource management (HRM). This paper explores how AI can be used in HRM, with a focus on important functions, including hiring, employee engagement, training and development, performance review, and retention. Chatbots, machine learning, natural language processing (NLP), and predictive analytics are examples of AI-powered technologies that increase productivity, reduce biases, and streamline HR operations. Despite the numerous benefits of artificial intelligence, issues such as algorithmic bias, data privacy, transparency, and resistance by employees still prevail. To assess AI's impact on HRM, the research employs a qualitative approach, analysing secondary data from scholarly articles, industry reports, and case studies. Findings indicate that while AI significantly enhances workforce management, ethical use and regulatory oversight are required. The research also considers possible future growth, with an emphasis on growth in AI, generative AI, and people analytics. Companies will achieve a competitive advantage in the evolving HR space if they thoroughly implement AI while maintaining human authority.

title: Understanding How AI-Assisted Evaluation Influences Innovative Processes, Collaboration, and Creative Confidence in Design Education
authors: Wang J.; Li J.; Zhu L.
abstract: Generative AI is increasingly embedded in design practice, yet its effects on convergent stages such as concept screening and selection remain underexplored in team settings. This study examines how a transparent AI co evaluator shapes screening practices, collaboration, and creative confidence in design education. We conducted a mixed-methods workshop where design student teams ranked ideas, then reconsidered choices after AI feedback. ProSight is a co-evaluator that returns rubric scores with brief evidence-linked rationales from each concept’s image and description. Teams reviewed the feedback, discussed agreement and conflict, and finalized selections. Data sources included ranking trajectories, pre post surveys on trust in AI, teamwork collaboration, and creative confidence, as well as post task discussions and interaction logs. Across groups, AI input rarely replaced initial preferences, but it shifted how options were compared and justified by making evaluative criteria more explicit and surfacing considerations that were less salient in early deliberation. Participants treated the AI as a credible reference for reflection and justification, but verified suggestions against intent and constraints, and kept authority over trade-offs and final decisions. The findings clarify how explanation rich AI can support reflective screening while reshaping collaborative dynamics in time limited group decision making.

title: Encouraging Thought Before Completion: The Role of Task-Specific Selective Friction in AI-Assisted Knowledge Work
authors: Arun S.K.; Fischer J.E.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded in knowledge work, raising concerns about how workers maintain agency, judgment, and accountability when AI assistance is readily available. This paper examines task-specific selective friction: lightweight, task-aligned preparatory actions that precede access to AI assistance. We conducted a mixed-methods study (N=40) comparing friction and no-friction conditions in literature review and brainstorming tasks. While preparatory friction significantly increased perceived mental demand, it also increased trust in and perceived usefulness of the AI, without degrading overall user experience. Contrary to expectations, friction did not reduce self-reported reliance on AI or increase critical evaluation. However, qualitative findings reveal that reliance and scrutiny are not opposing states but co-existing practices, shaped by task stakes and a sense of authorship over the work. We conceptualise this dynamic as conscious reliance, in which preparatory friction helps reposition AI from an unquestioned authority to a collaborative partner. Our findings suggest task-aligned friction as a design strategy for supporting more intentional and responsible Human-AI collaboration in knowledge work settings.

query_string: TITLE-ABS-KEY(("generative AI" OR "large language model" OR ChatGPT) AND (authority OR deference))
title: From Classroom to Enterprise: Architectural Patterns for LLM Integration
authors: Moriarty B.
abstract: Large language models are rapidly diffusing into academic and enterprise knowledge work, yet most deployments lack explicit collaboration architectures, leading to inconsistent outcomes, unclear accountability, and unresolved risk exposure. Organizations respond with opposing approaches: academic institutions impose prohibitions or detection mechanisms to preserve the integrity of the author, while enterprises mandate usage to accelerate productivity. Both approaches fail because they regulate behavior without defining how humans and LLMs should collaborate within actual workflows.This paper proposes centaur and cyborg frameworks as distinct human-LLM interaction patterns that differ in authority allocation, control boundaries, and failure modes. Centaur architectures maintain explicit decision boundaries with human authority over validation and final decisions, while cyborg architectures enable continuous collaboration with distributed oversight and supervisory control. We ground these frameworks in parallel longitudinal observations from academic (graduate data visualization course, seven semesters 2022-2025) and enterprise (software engineering and business operations) contexts, documenting remarkably similar evolution across three phases: novelty-driven atomic usage, stark shift to delegated patterns, and eventual differentiation into stable collaboration architectures. Both environments show atomic usage as the dominant pattern, with substantial subsets exhibiting centaur-aligned and degradedcentaur patterns, and small minorities demonstrating emergent cyborg usage.The convergence of patterns across contexts with opposing governance mechanisms suggests that these architectures represent recurring patterns observed in contrasting contexts rather than context-specific adaptations. We translate these observations into practical deployment guidance that emphasizes maturity-gated adoption, selection of risk-tiered architecture, and lightweight embedded controls over enforcement-based policies. Contribution is an architectural framework for designing, evaluating, and governing LLM-enabled workflows grounded in observed collaboration behaviors.

title: Reimagining work in the age of intelligent automation: a qualitative inquiry into AI-augmented workforce dynamics and managerial redesign
authors: Barbosa I.; de Oliveira E.R.
abstract: Purpose – This paper aims to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes contemporary work by augmenting, rather than substituting, human roles, engaging explicitly with substitution, augmentation and co-evolutionary perspectives on AI and the future of work. It introduces the concept of augmented work agency to refine sociotechnical debates on agency, control and coordination in AI-mediated settings and investigates how AI integration transforms managerial practices, workforce identities and organizational coordination, within evolving infrastructures that combine predictive and generative AI. Design/methodology/approach – A qualitative interpretivist research design was used, drawing on semistructured interviews with 28 managers and professionals from 12 organizations across technology, finance and knowledge-intensive service sectors in Europe and Asia. Using thematic and interpretive analysis, supported by organizational document review, the study identifies patterns of adaptation in organizations implementing AI at strategic and operational levels, paying particular attention to experiences of technostress, anxiety and the micro-political negotiation of AI tools in everyday work. Findings – This study develops an emergent framework of AI–human co-adaptation, illustrating how cognitive, relational and structural changes accompany AI integration across three interrelated dimensions: technological alignment, cognitive calibration and ethical anchoring. It uncovers three central tensions − autonomy versus orchestration, capability versus dependency and experimentation versus ethics − that collectively shape the evolving dynamics of AI‐mediated work and condition how organizations navigate competing priorities while fostering productive human–AI collaboration, and how employees experience and contest AI integration through forms of individual and collective agency. Originality/value – This paper advances understanding of augmented workforce design by introducing the concept of augmented work agency as a multi-level, interpretive form of human agency in algorithmically mediated environments, extending sociotechnical systems, algorithmic management and institutional-logics perspectives on agency, control and coordination. It conceptualizes AI as a co-evolving organizational capability rather than a deterministic technology and shows how augmented work agency is shaped by generative and non-generative AI applications, employees’ experiences of anxiety and technostress and the micro-politics through which teams and employee groups negotiate the boundaries of AI use and AI ethics. The study offers actionable insights for leaders seeking to balance innovation, capability development and ethical governance in AI-enabled workplaces while sustaining human interpretive authority, accountability and responsibility over time.

title: Distributed Teaching Agency–AI in the University: A Typology Based on Student Voice
authors: Fontaines-Ruiz T.; Ponce-Rojo A.; Merchan P.F.; Urcos W.C.; Rincon L.C.
abstract: Generative AI is reshaping university teaching and creating tension around authority, evidence, and accountability when decisions are made using algorithms. From a student perspective, this study constructed a typology of distributed teacher–AI agency (TAI) and examined the discursive mechanisms that produce the illusion of teacher autonomy. A non-experimental, cross-sectional, explanatory study was conducted: a lexicometric analysis of the ALCESTE (IRAMUTEQ) questionnaire, using open-ended responses from 3120 students (Mexico, n = 2051; Ecuador, n = 1069), segmented into 1077 units, and analyzed using positioning theory. Co-agency was operationalized using Teacher Agency (A), Delegation to AI (D), Governance (G: disclosure, criteria, verification), and the Illusion Index (II = A/(D + G + 1)). Three configurations emerged: Immediate Customizer (28.8%) with very high A and minimal D/G (II = 25.4); Technological Literacy Facilitator (27.3%) with visible delegation and safeguards (II ≈ 2.0); and Operational Optimizer (43.9%) oriented toward accelerating tasks with moderate governance (II ≈ 2.7). The illusion was associated with the agentive erasure of AI and a rhetoric of immediacy/efficiency that replaced verifiable criteria. These findings transform the student voice into a criteria-based diagnostic tool for strengthening traceability, minimal verification, and responsible orchestration of AI in higher education.

title: Framework for an Intelligent Reliability Engineering Assistant: A Rag-Based Genai Approach Leveraging Python Containers to Assist Reliability Engineering in Industrial Automation
authors: Jazdi N.; Maucher R.; Koch M.
abstract: Reliability analysis is a fundamental activity in the development and operation of industrial automation systems. Established methods such as Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA), Fault Tree Analysis (FTA), and Reliability Block Diagrams (RBDs) rely heavily on expert knowledge, normative standards and documents, and heterogeneous technical data sources. In recent years, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in information retrieval, reasoning, and natural language interaction. However, their direct application in reliability engineering is limited by issues such as hallucinations, lack of domain specificity, and insufficient explainability. This paper proposes a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)-based approach that integrates GenAI with structured reliability data, normative knowledge, and analytical models. A modular, layered architecture is introduced that enables domainaware, method-specific assistance while preserving human responsibility in safety-critical decision-making, explicitly avoiding any transfer of autonomous decision authority to the AI system. A proof-of-concept implementation is discussed qualitatively to evaluate feasibility and benefits. Finally, the broader potential of GenAI in industrial automation is analyzed, highlighting opportunities and limitations for future research.

title: Now more than ever: the role of museum and archival objects in an age of generative artificial intelligence
authors: Spennemann D.H.R.
abstract: Purpose The purpose of this paper is to demonstrate that in a era of deepfakes, generative artificial intelligence (AI) and misinformation, physical objects in museum and archival collections gain renewed significance as anchors of truth and authenticity. As trust in traditional authorities declines and digital content becomes easier to manipulate, the tangible, verifiable nature of real objects offers a crucial counterbalance. Unlike digital media, objects allow for direct, multi-sensory engagement and possess unique ontic features – such as wear, residue and modifications – that affirm their provenance. Their authenticity can be confirmed through documentation, eyewitness accounts and scientific methods. Design/methodology/approach This paper is a deliberation, examining the interface between diminishment in museum authority, a rise in alternative “truths” and the emergence of deep fakes in the age of generative AI. Findings Museums, as custodians of these artefacts, play a vital role in sustaining credible historical narratives, particularly as conspiracy theories may increasingly target lesser-known items with unclear histories. To safeguard collections, institutions must adopt robust documentation standards – such as blockchain-secured metadata, forensic-style photographic records and transparent curatorial histories. Though resource-intensive, these measures help protect against future challenges to authenticity and bolster public trust. Museums must also embrace an expanded educational role, equipping visitors to critically navigate the digital misinformation landscape and appreciate the evidentiary value of authentic objects. As younger, AI-native generations gravitate toward digital experiences, well-documented duplicates may offer vital opportunities for tactile engagement. Originality/value The content of the paper reaffirms the centrality of tangible objects in museum holdings. It argues that the enduring value of museums depends on their ability to adapt, remain transparent and preserve physical evidence of the past in a world increasingly shaped by digital illusions and contested truths.

title: Multi-Agent Foundation Models for Urban Mobility: The Malmö Elderly Case
authors: Biscalchin A.; Sarkheyli E.; Sarkheyli-Hagele A.
abstract: Understanding travel behaviour is crucial for developing inclusive, adaptable transportation systems in ageing cities. Yet many public authorities lack the expertise and budget for advanced analytics. We present a modular, multi-agent framework that employs Large Language Models (LLMs) to lower the entry barrier to data-driven mobility analysis. The pipeline extracts interpretable, policy-oriented insights from unstructured survey data and outputs structured reports without manual coding. We demonstrate the approach using Malmö's 2023 travel survey for residents aged 65+, and benchmark its recommendations against those of (i) a single-agent LLM service (Single Agent), representative of current commercial offerings, and (ii) a human expert baseline (Human), both evaluated in a blinded expert review. The system achieves superior reasoning quality compared to the single-agent baseline, while performing slightly lower on interpretability and focus, and approaches expert-level quality overall - at a fraction of the cost and effort. Key constraints are the current lack of real-time data ingestion and dependence on proprietary commercial APIs. The study provides an open-source proof of concept showing how multi-agent LLMs can make urban mobility analytics more accessible, transparent, and timely. All code and evaluation materials are publicly available.

title: Human-AI Symbiosis in Essay Assessment: A Human-in-the-Loop Scoring Model for Engineering Education
authors: Budayawan K.; Ganefri; Anwar M.; Asmara D.; Agustiarmi W.; Kurniadi D.
abstract: Essay evaluation is significant in engineering education because it allows lecturers to evaluate students' conceptual comprehension, technical reasoning, argumentation, and ability to explain engineering problem-solving procedures. However, hand essay scoring is frequently time-consuming, cognitively demanding, and vulnerable to inconsistency, especially when grading criteria are not explicitly operationalised. Recent developments in automated essay scoring, huge language models, and generative AI have created prospects to help assessment; yet, entirely automated scoring may reduce transparency, ignore contextual judgement, and undermine lecturer authority in assessment decision-making. This work presents a conceptual and technically defined human-in-the-loop scoring model for AI-assisted essay assessment in engineering education. The model incorporates analytic rubrics, rubric-guided prompting, retrieval-based knowledge sources, AI-assisted preliminary scoring, scoring rationales, feedback generation, lecturer validation, and revision-aware final scoring. To provide operational clarity, the study defines the AI-assisted scoring pipeline in terms of structured inputs, retrieval-supported context, prompt components, output schema, uncertainty flagging, lecturer validation, and an audit trail. The study also describes a preliminary pilot evaluation that included anonymised essay replies from 30 students who answered four essay questions, yielding 120 essay-response units and 480 dimension-level scoring judgements. The evaluation compares GPT-4o-mini-generated preliminary results to lecturer-approved scores using precise agreement, adjacent agreement, mean absolute error, Cohen's Kappa, and Quadratic Weighted Kappa. In the suggested workflow, AI serves as a decision-support component, producing preliminary scores, rationales, feedback suggestions, and noted issues, while lecturers review, revise, and make final assessment decisions. The model is expected to support more transparent, consistent, and formative essay assessment while maintaining lecturer authority and human responsibility in educational assessment.

title: Standards-Aligned Ethical Gating and Decision Telemetry for LLM-Assisted Mobile Robot Navigation: A Simulation Study
authors: Pandit P.K.; Singh A.; Galiya H.B.; Wu W.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly considered for autonomous robot decision support, but their non-deterministic outputs are difficult to validate in safety-critical settings. This paper presents a governance architecture for mobile robot navigation that incorporates LLM reasoning as a bounded advisory component without granting it direct control authority. The architecture combines schema-constrained LLM outputs, deterministic arbitration, a hard safety gate at the actuation interface, and structured telemetry for post-hoc audit. Implemented in ROS 2 Jazzy and evaluated in Gazebo Harmonic, the system is tested across four scenarios spanning obstacle avoidance, privacy-boundary enforcement, and an ethical dilemma requiring the robot to balance competing privacy and mission-urgency obligations. Over 2,400 simulation trials, the architecture achieved zero safety violations and zero decision instability. LLM participation ranged from 87% to 96% across scenarios, with deterministic fallback compensating where model confidence was lower. In the dilemma scenario, the system produced graduated responses with explicit tradeoff reasoning rather than binary outcomes. The results demonstrate that deterministic enforcement combined with structured telemetry can provide both runtime safety and auditable evidence for responsible deployment of LLM-Assisted autonomous systems.

query_string: TITLE-ABS-KEY(("generative AI" OR "large language model" OR ChatGPT) AND (authority OR deference))
title: Debiasing and Explainability Effectiveness of LLM Tuning: A Quantitative Approach
authors: Mauri L.; Preda F.; Damiani E.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often perpetuate implicit biases from user prompts, necessitating fine-tuning to enhance fairness and explainability. However, quantifying tuning efficacy remains an open problem. This paper introduces a novel Shapley value-based framework to evaluate the debiasing impact by analyzing token attributions in prompts. We propose a dual metric - Shapley Bias Distribution (SBD, using the Gini coefficient) and Shapley Bias Entropy (SBE) - to measure the concentration of contributions, distinguishing between single-term and multiple-term biases. To streamline the analysis, we further propose the Focused SHAP Entropy Ratio (FSER), a composite metric that integrates Gini-like inequality and entropy-like uncertainty via core-periphery decomposition, with an automated threshold for unbiased, task-adaptive assessment. Our experiments on a Corpus of Linguistic Acceptability (CoLA)-inspired benchmark demonstrate lower variance and decreased entropy post-tuning, signaling a sharper focus on salient tokens and improved bias isolation. Our metrics enable rigorous verification of tuning outcomes, revealing incomplete debiasing through persistent high entropy. This provides certification authorities with a palette of tools that enhance trustworthiness and facilitate scalable certification.

title: A multilayered analysis of university students’ experiences with human and AI-based feedback: A comparative examination of BERTopic, LLM models, and mixture of agents approaches
authors: Yildiz Durak H.; Onan A.
abstract: This study presents a multilayered text analysis framework for examining university students’ experiences with human- and artificial intelligence (AI)-based feedback. The empirical corpus consisted of 322 feedback-related reflection statements obtained from 110 undergraduate students. The analysis combined data preprocessing, corpus-driven thematic modeling with BERTopic, zero-shot thematic extraction using large language models (LLMs), ensemble-based semantic alignment, psycholinguistic emotion–theme integration, and high-resolution thematic refinement through a Mixture of Agents (MoA) framework. BERTopic identified six core themes: trust and transparency, cognitive load and clarity, learning contribution and perceived benefit, emotional discomfort and uncertainty, human-AI comparison, and complementary feedback expectations. The results showed that students’ feedback experiences were multidimensional, involving cognitive, affective, explanatory, and comparative dimensions rather than a simple preference for either feedback source. BERTopic provided a stable corpus-grounded thematic baseline, whereas Large Language Model (LLM)-based zero-shot extraction produced pedagogically interpretable and conceptually expressive theme labels. The ensemble approach reduced variation across individual LLM outputs by consolidating semantically similar labels. MoA further refined thematic distinctions and improved emotion–topic alignment, particularly in statements involving cognitive ambiguity or emotionally charged feedback experiences. Comparative analyses indicated that AI-based feedback was more strongly associated with speed, accessibility, consistency, and immediate learning support, whereas human feedback was more strongly associated with contextual richness, empathy, pedagogical explanation, and perceived authority. The findings suggest that effective feedback design should combine the scalability and immediacy of AI-based feedback with human oversight, contextual interpretation, emotional calibration, and transparent justification. Overall, the study contributes to learning analytics and feedback research by demonstrating how corpus-driven topic modeling, LLM-based interpretation, ensemble alignment, and MoA-based refinement can be integrated to model the cognitive and affective dimensions of students’ feedback experiences.

title: Unmasking the Fake: Designing Explainable AI Agents for Autonomous Deepfake Mitigation
authors: Kumar P.S.; Ramanamurthy P.V.; Teja P.B.; Prasad M.S.L.; Mishra S.; Sunny G.S.
abstract: The fast progress of generative AI technologies has enabled the widespread generation and sharing of manipulated media, called deep fakes. These synthetic video and audio could ultimately undermine digital trust, privacy, and public safety. Many traditional systems for detecting deepfakes are black-box systems, providing limited transparency, interpretability, and real-world usability. The systems can be very limited in terms of explain ability and autonomous response, making it challenging for users, institutions, and authorities to validate authenticity, with timeliness, if needed.This paper introduces an Explainable AI-based Autonomous Deepfake Detection System that detects, interprets, and reasons about deepfake content in media files. The proposed system leverages MTCNN for face detection and InceptionResNetV1 for detecting deepfakes, using facial embeddings as classifiers. This system uses Gemini AI APIs, in two ways, as a modality to produce multimodal explanations for the detected outputs and uses Gemini's verification of evidence function through Google Search. The proposed architecture is also designed to analyze audio deepfakes, to detect manipulated voices and lip-sync mismatches, and to incorporate recommendations about evidence verification of manipulated content. Upon discovering possible deepfakes, the AI agent performs contextual actions on its own-providing human-readable explanations, searching for original content online, and documenting metadata and timestamps for compliance.

query_string: TITLE-ABS-KEY(("generative AI" OR "large language model" OR ChatGPT) AND (authority OR deference))
title: AI and higher education: teachers' perceptions of students' ethical tensions in online pedagogical methods
authors: Baoyi W.; Khan F.U.
abstract: The emergence and development of generative AI tools have benefited higher education but have also created several ethical tensions in the educational system. This tension is higher in online teaching environments, where students often rely on AI tools. Previous studies have addressed ethical issues, yet how these issues have emerged across various teaching methods in online AI-driven classes has been overlooked. To address this gap, this qualitative study investigates teachers' perceptions about their students' ethical issues across five pedagogical methodologies: direct method, content and language integrating learning, task-based language teaching, communicative language teaching, and community language learning. These five methods represent widely used approaches to second- or foreign-language teaching rather than instructional methods in general, and the findings are accordingly specific to language-acquisition classrooms. Using thematic analysis of interviews with 25 teachers, this research recognized 20 unique ethical tensions across five teaching methodologies. These findings are synthesized into a holistic framework comprising three overarching ethical domains: authenticity of learning, authority challenge, and collaborative dynamics. Based on this framework, this research highlights the need for moving beyond general frameworks to method-based ethical policies in education. This research emphasizes a process-oriented assessment framework to ensure transparency in education and mitigate the risk of unethical issues and tensions in the educational system. Further implications for students, teachers, and policy makers have been discussed.

query_string: TITLE-ABS-KEY(("generative AI" OR "large language model" OR ChatGPT) AND (authority OR deference))
title: KnowPath: An LLM-Supported Knowledge Graph Construction and Path Finding Framework to Explainable MOOC Recommendations
authors: Zhu J.; Chen Z.; Meo P.D.; Guan J.; Han Z.; Shi W.
abstract: The proliferation of Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) has created an urgent need for advanced course recommendation systems (RS). Course recommendations in MOOCs require transparent motivations to justify course selection, as there are often many courses with the same title, but which vary widely in content, duration, learning resources provided, and the academic authority of the instructor. Explainable recommendations are crucial to ensure that recommended courses fit well with learners’ needs and increase the chance of successful course completion, but unfortunately existing RS for MOOCs struggle to provide explainable recommendations. In this article, we present KnowPath, a novel RS for MOOCs, which generates effective and explainable recommendations. KnowPath uses open source Large Language Models (LLMs) to construct knowledge graphs (KGs) capable of accurately capturing complex relationships between MOOC entities (e.g., learners, instructors, educational resources) and employs Reinforcement Learning to align the output of an LLM with learner preferences. Extensive experiments on two public datasets (XueTang and COCO) demonstrate the superior performance and generalizability of KnowPath, underlining its potential to revolutionize the field of personalized online education.

title: Hegemonikon and AI
authors: Koutsotasios C.A.; Vavouras E.
abstract: The central ethical problem raised by artificial intelligence is not whether AI systems can “reason” in a functional sense, but whether their use preserves a centre of judgment that can be held responsible. Beginning with large language models, it distinguishes linguistic fluency from scientific validity, ethical commitment, and accountability. Enter the Stoic concept of the hegemonikon-the capacity for assent that directs the mind-as a framework for understanding intellectual creation and decision-making. This framework is extended by analogy to institutions clarifying when AI supports human judgment and when it replaces decision-making authority. The argument is applied to various fields and leads to five principles for the ethical use of AI: disclosure, attribution, critical engagement with AI outputs, meaningful human oversight, and augmentation rather than replacement. Responsible AI governance requires institutions to preserve decision-making structures that are identifiable, open to challenge and revision, and subject to accountability.<sup>1</sup>.

title: Emerging frontiers and challenges of artificial intelligence in PSMA-PET imaging: pioneering a new chapter in prostate cancer care
authors: Wang Y.; Cheng C.; Huang B.; Zuo C.
abstract: Prostate-specific membrane antigen positron emission tomography (PSMA-PET) has become pivotal in prostate cancer (PCa) management, offering superior sensitivity over conventional imaging for detecting tumors, metastases, and biochemical recurrence. However, interpretive subjectivity, workflow inefficiencies, and heterogeneous PSMA expression remain significant limitations. Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly radiomics and deep learning, addresses these challenges by enabling automated lesion analysis and image enhancement. This review examines the impact of AI across the PSMA-PET workflow, covering optimized image acquisition (e.g., low-dose protocols, motion correction), enhanced interpretation (e.g., lesion characterization, prognostic stratification), and personalized theranostics (e.g., treatment response forecasting, radioligand therapy dosimetry). Despite promising multicenter validation, challenges remain in annotation standardization, data heterogeneity, model generalizability, interpretability, regulatory integration, and ethics. We further discuss emerging frontiers, including multimodal multi-omic integration, generative AI, and AI-driven clinical decision support systems. Notably, we highlight the evolving role of nuclear medicine physicians and radiologists as integrators of AI-derived biomarkers, who validate AI outputs for high-stakes decisions, retain interpretive authority for complex cases, and oversee quality assurance, ensuring that AI augments rather than replaces specialist expertise. These advances position AI-integrated PSMA-PET to drive precision oncology, with key pathways outlined for clinical translation and future innovation in PCa care.

title: Readability, information quality, and safety of AI chatbot responses to common questions about ostomy care: A cross-sectional digital health evaluation
authors: Zhang Y.; Li X.; Su J.; Yuan L.I.; Zhou A.; Chen L.; Zhang H.
abstract: Background: Patients with ostomies often require timely, understandable, and reliable guidance for self-care after surgery. Although AI chatbots are increasingly used as accessible sources of health information, the quality and safety of their responses for ostomy care remain uncertain. Objective: To compare information quality, readability, and text-level safety across five chatbots answering common ostomy-care questions. Methods: We submitted forty-six matched patient-facing ostomy-care questions once to five chatbots (ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity AI, DeepSeek, and Doubao) through official web interfaces on March 31, 2026, yielding 230 first responses. Responses were assessed with DISCERN, EQIP, Global Quality Score (GQS), JAMA benchmarks, six readability indices, and a guideline-based audit. Citation review was limited to Perplexity AI, the only system displaying source links. Comparisons used Friedman, Wilcoxon, and Cochran’s Q tests with multiplicity adjustment. Results: Scores differed across all four measures of quality and all six readability indices after Holm correction (adjusted P<.001). Perplexity AI in Pro Search mode scored higher on DISCERN, EQIP, and JAMA. Of its 1,721 citations, 18.9% were nonacademic or low-authority and 5.3% clinically inappropriate. DeepSeek had lower reading-grade estimates, but no system met the sixth-grade benchmark. Agreement was good for quantitative scores (ICC [2,1] =0.758–0.791) and high for qualitative coding (κ=0.830–0.842). Guideline deviations and potential text-level safety risks occurred across systems, with no significant adjusted between-system differences. Conclusions: None was consistently suitable as a stand-alone source of ostomy education. Their responses may support patient education after professional review but should not replace clinician-guided instruction.
